title: Lyddie (Selected Chapters & The Industrial Mill Experience)
author: Katherine Paterson

sections.heading: The Bear in the Cabin & Vermont Hardship

epigraph.quote: We can, Lyddie thought. We can make it. She stared down the bear, standing between her mother and the open door.

paragraphs: Thirteen-year-old Lyddie Worthen was born into hardship on a hillside Vermont farm. With her father having deserted the family years earlier to seek his fortune in the West, the family was left deeply in debt. In the opening chapter, a black bear enters their small log cabin through the open door, searching for food. While her fearful mother and younger siblings flee into the loft, Lyddie courageously stands her ground, staring down the bear and saving her family.

Despite her bravery, her superstitious mother decides the bear is a sign of the end of the world. She leases the farm to pay creditors and hires Lyddie out as an indentured servant at Cutler's Tavern for fifty cents a week. Determined to earn enough money to pay off the family debt and reunite her family on the farm, Lyddie resolves to take control of her destiny.

sections.heading: The Lowell Mills: Deafening Looms and Factory Speeds

epigraph.quote: The noise was like a thundering waterfall of iron and wood, shaking the floor beneath her boots until her teeth vibrated.

paragraphs: Hearing from a friendly traveler about the high cash wages offered to 'factory girls' in Massachusetts, Lyddie escapes the tavern and travels to Lowell. Hired at the Concord Corporation weaving mill, she enters an alien industrial world. Thirteen hours a day, six days a week, Lyddie tends multiple mechanical looms in an enclosed weaving room choked with airborne lint, with windows nailed shut to keep humidity high.

Lyddie works with ferocious intensity, quickly becoming the fastest weaver in the corporation and taking on four looms at once. But the brutal conditions take a heavy toll: girls succumb to 'mill fever' and lung disease, machinery amputates fingers, and the corporation speeds up the looms while cutting piece-rate wages.

sections.heading: The Ten-Hour Petition and Choosing Autonomy

epigraph.quote: She had not been broken. She was going to Ohio. She would attend college. She was free.

paragraphs: When her roommate Diana Goss invites Lyddie to join the Female Labor Reform Association and sign a petition to the state legislature demanding a ten-hour workday, Lyddie resists. Terrified of being blacklisted and losing her wages, she tells herself that work is work and that she must look out only for herself and her brother Charlie.

However, after witnessing overseer Mr. Marsden mistreat younger workers and having herself discharged dishonorably without a certificate of good character for defending a friend, Lyddie realizes that economic security means nothing without human dignity. Instead of returning defeated to Vermont or accepting an unloving marriage proposal, Lyddie decides to journey west to Oberlin College in Ohio. She chooses freedom, intellectual independence, and self-determination.
